The teacher\'s cipher, and where Codex comes from.
Codex began with a civics test. The teacher had brought a photograph of a cipher table — an alphabet, syllables, names, signs that meant nothing at all — and the test on that table went badly.

That same afternoon, in two hours, a small program appeared: it enciphered a sentence and turned it into an image, so a friend could get an answer nobody else could read. That program became this app.
Of the table, though, the first version took only the shape. It reduced it to a numeric correspondence and threw away the way the cipher actually worked. This section exists to put that right.
It is not a substituted alphabet. It is a nomenclator, and it is five things at once. They are all in the photograph below.

Twenty-two letters: a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t v x y z. There is no u, because v did the work of both. The most frequent letters have more than one sign, stacked underneath: they are the ones an attacker counts first.
Fifteen consonants by five vowels, from ba be bi bo bu down to za ze zi zo zu, with the q row written qua que qui quo quu. Seventy-five signs worth two letters each.
bb cc dd ff gg ll mm nn pp rr ss tt uu. Thirteen of them, and Italian is full of doubles.

Pope, Emperor, King of France, Pisa, Florence, Army, Tomorrow, Salvestro, Sums, Germany. The words that came back in every dispatch, each with its own sign. This is the part the whole system is named after.
Nine signs that mean nothing, scattered through the text so that whoever intercepts it counts wrong.
The signs below are not the flourishes in the manuscript. The structure is: counted off the photograph, with the same letters, syllables, doubles and words.
il papa scrive domani a firenze
What each sign stands for appears underneath it.

resources.string: The signs are built the way the chanceries built theirs: a shape, with a dot or a bar above or below that makes it mean something else. Forty shapes are enough to fill a table of a hundred and twenty entries.
We still know nothing certain about the table: not which archive it comes from, nor which chancery used it.

What can be read in the photograph does say something. Among the nomenclator words, Pisa and Florence appear as separate entries, next to the Emperor, the King of France and the Army, and further on Germany: a Tuscan chancery during the Italian Wars, between 1494 and 1530, with Pisa in revolt. Salvestro is a Florentine given name. It is a reading, not an attribution.
The shortest path is still to ask the teacher where the image came from. The others are these.
None of these sources has identified the document yet. When one does, this page will say so, with the name of the archive and the shelfmark.

There is no secret in here: your name, your mineral and your public keys, signed. You can send it in a message without a second thought.
Two ways, depending on where you are

Then it is their turn to scan yours: both cards are needed.
Agree on a word out loud, face to face or on the phone. Do not type it in here and do not send it in a chat: it is the one thing that must never cross a screen.
Accents, capitals and punctuation do not count.
That was not enough. Try the whole word.
Are you both seeing the same gem?
The word makes the key, and the key makes the gem. If you heard different words, you will see different gems.
If the two gems match, the conversation is yours and nobody else\'s. If they differ, something went wrong: do the rite again.

When one of your contacts is in the same room, messages go straight from one phone to the other. No internet, no server, no account.
They start with the app and stop when you close it.
Even with the screen off. The system shows a notification while they run.

To find nearby phones Android asks for these permissions. Codex does not use them to know where you are: they are for finding devices in the room, and on older phones Android still calls that "location".
Without those permissions nearby stays off. Everything else in Codex works the same.

Your phone needs a lock: fingerprint, PIN or pattern. Without one there is nothing to ask whether it is you.
Who else receives this account\'s notifications. A notification contains nothing, but it does say something arrived.
It stops receiving notifications. If that phone is still yours and you open Codex on it, it will register again: to remove it for good, disconnect the account from there.
Removes your profile, your directory entry and your devices from the server

Gone from the server: your public profile, other people\'s ability to find you, the registered devices, the mail and the stories.
Staying on this phone: identity, contacts and messages, all readable. Staying in other people\'s conversations: the envelopes already delivered, which expire on their own after thirty days — those are not ours to delete.
There is no going back.
